query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA, the degradation mechanism during high-temperature exposure is governed by the reactive gas environment. Specifically, under high oxygen partial pressures selective oxidation of elements (notably Al, Cr, and Ti) forms a continuous, albeit compositionally graded, oxide scale that partially protects the matrix, whereas under reducing conditions the suppression of this scale formation accelerates elemental segregation and phase destabilization, triggering brittle phase formation and leading to catastrophic failure.
generation.material_initial_state: An additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA with a fine, non-equilibrium FCC matrix produced by rapid solidification, featuring a relatively homogeneous elemental distribution prior to exposure.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the oxygen partial pressure of the heating atmosphere from strongly oxidizing (high O2 content) to strongly reducing (high H2, CO, or low O2 levels) while maintaining constant high-temperature exposure.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted at temperatures above 700°C for fixed durations (e.g., 10–12 hours) with the only variable being the controlled gas composition (oxygen partial pressure) in the test chamber.
generation.structural_mediator: The nature and morphology of the oxide scale that forms at the alloy surface and the degree of elemental segregation at the oxide/substrate interface.
generation.mechanism: Under oxidizing conditions, selective oxidation of Al, Cr, and Ti yields a relatively uniform and adherent oxide scale that slows further degradation; under reducing conditions, the lack of robust oxide scale formation fosters uneven elemental diffusion and segregation, destabilizing the FCC matrix. This leads to the formation of brittle phases and local microstructural defects (e.g., intergranular cracks) that coalesce into catastrophic failure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples exposed to high oxygen partial pressures will develop a thicker, more homogeneous oxide scale with minimal internal segregation and reduced crack initiation, while samples in reducing atmospheres will exhibit discontinuous or thinner oxide layers, pronounced elemental segregation, early brittle phase formation, and increased microcrack density.
generation.baseline: The as-built alloy state with a fine, non-equilibrium FCC matrix and uniform elemental distribution before any high-temperature exposure.
generation.boundary: Findings apply to high-temperature conditions (>700°C) under controlled gas compositions ranging from oxidizing (e.g., ambient air or enriched oxygen) to reducing (e.g., high H2 or CO environments) atmospheres.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative thresholds (e.g., oxide thickness, segregation levels, critical oxygen partial pressures) at which the transition between protective oxidation and deleterious phase destabilization occurs remain to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of identical as-built samples and expose them at >700°C for a fixed duration while systematically varying the oxygen partial pressure—from strongly oxidizing to reducing conditions. Post-exposure, perform cross‐sectional characterization using SEM/EDS and XRD to assess oxide scale uniformity, measure elemental segregation profiles, identify any new phase formation, and quantify crack density.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and spatial uniformity
Elemental mapping of the oxide/substrate interface (EDS)
Phase identification (XRD) to detect formation of brittle compounds
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If altering the oxygen partial pressure does not result in significant and reproducible differences in oxide scale morphology, degree of elemental segregation, or crack initiation relative to the as-built baseline, then the hypothesis that the gas chemistry (via selective oxidation versus phase destabilization) governs the degradation process is falsified.

AbstractThe oxidation behavior of an equimolar Cr-Mn-Fe-Co high-entropy alloy (HEA) processed by 3D laser printing was investigated at 700 °C and 900 °C. The oxidation kinetics of the alloy followed the parabolic rate law, and the oxidation rate constant increased with the rising of the temperature. Inward diffusion of oxygen and outward diffusion of cations took place during the high-temperature oxidation process. A spinel-type oxide was formed on the surface, and the thickness of the oxide layer increased with the rising of experimental temperature or time. The exfoliation of the oxide layer took place when the test was operated at 900 °C over 12 h. During oxidation tests, the matrix was propped open by oxides and was segmented into small pieces. The formation of loose structures had great effects on the high-temperature oxidation resistance of the HEA.Keywords: metals and alloys, 3D printing, oxidation

frame.system: Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, initially produced with a fine, non-equilibrium microstructure from rapid solidification.
frame.goal: To understand and explain the mechanistic origin of degradation under elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing environments, including the onset of catastrophic failure.
frame.limitation: There is an incomplete understanding of how the alloy’s microstructure evolves under different gas chemistries at high temperatures and how changes such as selective oxidation, phase partitioning, or elemental segregation trigger rapid, catastrophic degradation.
constraints: Must propose a controlled change (e.g., systematically adjusting the gas chemistry from oxidizing to reducing or altering O2 partial pressure) relative to the baseline as-fabricated alloy
Predictions should compare the post-exposure observations (e.g., oxide scale morphology, microstructural phase evolution, crack propagation patterns) to the starting state
Applicable temperature and time exposures should be clearly bounded (for example, experiments performed above 700°C over set intervals)

The hypothesis should be supported by prior evidence from studies on similar high-entropy alloys or conventional alloys where microstructural evolution under reactive atmospheres was correlated with degradation

A clear falsification criterion must be included (for instance, if controlled gas composition change does not yield the predicted differences in oxide scale uniformity or microstructural partitions, the hypothesis would be rejected)
frame.regime: High-temperature conditions (e.g., T > 700°C) under controlled oxidizing (e.g., high O2 partial pressure) and reducing (e.g., high H2 or CO environments) atmospheres, with well-defined exposure durations.
prior_attempts: Earlier work on similar high-entropy systems and conventional alloys indicated that under oxidizing conditions, selective oxidation (especially of Al, Cr, or Ti) leads to protective vs. non-protective oxide scales. However, these studies typically did not isolate the role of additive manufacturing–induced microstructural heterogeneities, nor did they examine the effects of switching to reducing environments. Consequently, a direct correlation between these microstructural features and catastrophic failure via oxidation-induced embrittlement or phase destabilization remains unresolved.

decision.trend: Early work on additively manufactured and post‐processed high-entropy alloys (HEAs) – especially Al-containing systems – has shown that the non-equilibrium microstructure resulting from rapid solidification tends to produce fine secondary phases (e.g., nitrides and intermetallics) that can evolve upon thermal exposure. Studies have explored how heat treatment modifies phase fractions and elemental partitioning, and other work on conventional alloys has correlated selective oxidation (particularly of key elements like Al, Cr, or Ti) with the formation—or disruption—of protective oxide scales. However, prior experiments mostly varied annealing temperatures without isolating the role of reactive gas composition. As a result, while the benefits and limits of scaled oxide formation (versus deleterious elemental segregation or phase destabilization) have been partially mapped, the direct link between controlled gas environment, microstructural evolution, and the onset of catastrophic failure remains unsolved.
decision.unsolved: It remains unclear whether degradation and the ensuing catastrophic failure are governed primarily by selective oxidation that alters the protective nature of the oxide scale (leading to embrittlement and crack propagation) or by a gas-driven trigger for phase partitioning and elemental segregation in the inherently heterogeneous microstructure produced by additive manufacturing. In other words, the specific mechanistic role of oxidizing versus reducing atmospheres in driving microstructural instabilities is unresolved.
decision.lever: Systematically vary the gas composition—specifically, modulate the oxygen partial pressure over a controlled range (from strongly oxidizing to reducing conditions) at fixed high-temperature conditions (e.g., >700°C for set durations)—and monitor the evolution of the oxide scale morphology, phase distribution, and crack initiation behavior relative to the as-built baseline.
decision.why: This approach directly follows from the trend where earlier studies modified thermal histories but did not isolate reactive gas effects. By controlling the O2 partial pressure, the experiment will test whether selective oxidation (or its suppression) governs the degradation mechanism. Predicted observations include the formation of a continuous, possibly protective, oxide scale under high O2 conditions versus localized oxide breakdown, enhanced elemental segregation, and initiation of microcracks under reducing conditions. The falsification criterion is clear: if the systematic change in gas composition does not yield the predicted differences in oxide scale uniformity, microstructural partitioning, and crack propagation patterns compared to the starting state, then the hypothesis (that the gas chemistry controls degradation mechanism) would be rejected.
